name: El Imposible National Park
blurb: Wet mountain forest where fruit trees feed bats and birds, and pumas hunt.

tip.title: Take away the rains
tip.text: Rain keeps the forest plants growing. Set Seasonal rain to -100% and watch the fruit plants fail, then the bats, birds and the cats above them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the forest canopy powers the growth of the trees and shrubs that feed the whole web.

nodes.name: Seasonal rain
nodes.desc: Rain feeds the rivers of the watershed and keeps this tropical mountain forest wet enough for lush plant growth.

nodes.name: Forest soil nutrients
nodes.desc: Nutrients in the soil of the volcanic mountain slopes are taken up by the roots of forest plants.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, fruit and dead animals, returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: West Indian milkberry
nodes.desc: A shrub or climber with small white berries. GloBI records show bats, doves, thrushes and other birds eating its fruit.

nodes.name: Alligatorwood
nodes.desc: A common tree of the forest understorey in the GBIF records here. Birds such as manakins and thrushes are recorded eating its fruit.

nodes.name: Wax mallow
nodes.desc: A shrub with red tubular flowers and fleshy fruit. Manakins and thrushes are recorded eating the fruit.

nodes.name: Jamaican fruit bat
nodes.desc: A fruit-eating bat that carries fruit to a roost and so spreads seeds. Boa constrictors are among its listed predators.

nodes.name: Long-tailed manakin
nodes.desc: The most recorded bird near the site. It eats small fruits such as those of alligatorwood and wax mallow.

nodes.name: Clay-colored thrush
nodes.desc: A widespread thrush that eats fruit, recorded on milkberry, alligatorwood and wax mallow.

nodes.name: White-tipped dove
nodes.desc: A ground-feeding dove of forest floor and edges. It is recorded eating the berries of West Indian milkberry.

nodes.name: Deppe's squirrel
nodes.desc: A tree squirrel of tropical forests that eats fruit and seeds. Recorded within the circle around the site.

nodes.name: Mexican deer mouse
nodes.desc: A small rodent of montane forests. It eats seeds, fruit and insects and is prey for snakes and small cats.

nodes.name: Giant red-winged grasshopper
nodes.desc: A very large tropical grasshopper that chews leaves, and is prey for lizards and birds.

nodes.name: Central American boa
nodes.desc: A constrictor that eats mammals, lizards and birds. GloBI records Jamaican fruit bats as prey.

nodes.name: Squirrel cuckoo
nodes.desc: A long-tailed forest cuckoo that hunts large insects in the canopy and also eats fruit, such as milkberry.

nodes.name: Rainbow ameiva
nodes.desc: A fast ground lizard of forest floors that forages for insects and other small invertebrates.

nodes.name: Lesson's motmot
nodes.desc: A large forest bird that eats insects, small lizards and fruit.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: Feeds almost entirely on carrion, finding it largely by smell, and so helps clear dead animals from the forest.

nodes.name: Black vulture
nodes.desc: A scavenger that feeds on carcasses and often crowds out turkey vultures at a carcass.

nodes.name: Puma
nodes.desc: Named among the large predators of El Imposible. In El Salvador it has been recorded in montane forest, and it hunts small to medium mammals.

nodes.name: Oncilla
nodes.desc: A small forest cat that hunts rodents, lizards, birds, eggs and invertebrates, and climbs well. Listed for El Imposible.
